_comment: Naming traditions authored in UHS, merged with the vendored HPG sets by scripts/port-name-kits.ts. An id here replaces an HPG set of the same id. Every entry needs an era, at least one source, and a note saying what the pool is drawn from. No entry may be a place name, ethnonym, deity, title, common noun, or a person who died after 1900 — src/content/characters/name-entries.ts enforces that.

old-norse.label: Old Norse
old-norse.note: Given names from the Scandinavian runic corpus, which begins in the migration period, and from the Icelandic family sagas. There were no surnames: a person was named for their father, with -sson or -sdottir, and that element was not inherited.

sami-north.label: Northern Sami
sami-north.note: Names recorded in Nordic church books and tax rolls from the sixteenth century onward, in their Sami rather than Norwegianised forms. Sami naming used a personal name plus a parent's name; hereditary surnames were imposed later by state registration.

komi-permic.label: Komi and Permic
komi-permic.note: Komi personal names as they appear in Novgorodian and Muscovite tribute registers, where indigenous names stand beside the Orthodox baptismal names that progressively replaced them. Russian-form surnames are a feature of the imperial period and are omitted.

ob-ugric.label: Khanty and Mansi
ob-ugric.note: Khanty and Mansi personal names from Siberian tribute registers and Finno-Ugric ethnographic record. Names were often taken from the natural world or from circumstances of birth; hereditary surnames arrived with Russian administration.

old-turkic.label: Old Turkic
old-turkic.note: Names from the Orkhon and Yenisei runiform inscriptions of the Turk and Uyghur khaganates. Rank words such as khan, tegin and tarkan are titles and are not used here as names.

japanese-classical.label: Japanese, Nara to Edo
japanese-classical.note: Commoners in Japan did not generally carry surnames until the registration law of 1875; a personal name alone, often marking birth order for men, is the ordinary case. Warrior and court names are drawn from Heian and Kamakura records.

angkorian-khmer.label: Angkorian Khmer
angkorian-khmer.note: Names from Old Khmer and Sanskrit temple inscriptions, which record servants and estate workers as well as kings. Angkorian Khmer had no hereditary surname.

anglo-colonial-diaspora.label: African-descended, Anglo-American colonies
anglo-colonial-diaspora.note: Names recorded in Anglo-American plantation inventories and runaway advertisements. Three strands run together: Akan day-names carried from West Africa, English diminutives, and classical or place names imposed by owners. Enslaved people were recorded without surnames, though many used names among themselves that the records do not preserve.

icelandic.label: Icelandic
icelandic.note: Icelanders carry no hereditary surname. A person is named for a parent — Jónsson or Jónsdóttir — so the second element changes with each generation and differs between a brother and a sister.

prehistoric-proto-indo-european.label: Reconstructed Proto-Indo-European
prehistoric-proto-indo-european.note: Two-part names built from reconstructed Proto-Indo-European roots — fame, horse, cattle, king, people, god — in the compounding pattern that the attested daughter languages all inherit. No Indo-European personal name survives from this period; these are the shape such a name would take, not recovered individuals.

prehistoric-proto-celtic.label: Reconstructed Proto-Celtic
prehistoric-proto-celtic.note: Compounds of Proto-Celtic elements attested in later Gaulish, British and Irish names — catu- battle, rix- king, vindo- white, touto- people, epo- horse, maglo- chief. Built as plausible La Tene-era forms rather than taken from the named chieftains of Roman accounts.

prehistoric-proto-germanic.label: Reconstructed Proto-Germanic
prehistoric-proto-germanic.note: Two-element names in the Germanic pattern preserved by the earliest runic inscriptions and Roman-era transcriptions — hathu- battle, theud- people, hroth- fame, hild- war, gund- battle. The floor is set at the point Proto-Germanic is distinguishable; earlier dates are a different language and are left uncovered.

prehistoric-mena.label: Early Dynastic Egyptian
prehistoric-mena.note: Names of officials, priests and their households recorded on Early Dynastic and early Old Kingdom seals, stelae and mastaba walls. Egyptians carried no family name. Nothing before about 3400 BCE is recoverable, so earlier dates are left uncovered rather than filled with the names of archaeological sites.

prehistoric-african.label: Bantu-pattern reconstruction
prehistoric-african.note: Short forms built to Bantu sound patterns — open syllables, prenasalised stops, no final consonant — using the shape of names recorded across the Bantu-speaking world rather than any one language. This period leaves no written record anywhere in Central or Southern Africa; the pattern is the reconstruction, not the people.

levantine.label: Levantine, modern
levantine.note: Given names and family names in general use across Lebanon, Syria and Palestine, drawn from both Christian and Muslim naming stocks. Family names are occupational or descriptive in origin and became hereditary under Ottoman and Mandate registration.

great-basin-native.label: Numic-pattern reconstruction
great-basin-native.note: Forms built to Numic sound patterns — simple syllables, doubled consonants, the diminutive ending -tsi — shared by Shoshone, Paiute and Ute. Great Basin peoples took names from events and visions and changed them through life. These are constructed shapes, not words or names from any of those languages.

creek-muskogee.label: Muskogean-pattern reconstruction
creek-muskogee.note: Forms built to Muskogean sound patterns. A Creek person's public name was usually a war title earned in adulthood, attached to their town and matrilineal clan — Hopothle, Yahola, Tustunnuggee are ranks rather than names, and are not used here. These are constructed shapes, not words from Mvskoke.

muisca.label: Muisca, Chibcha-pattern
muisca.note: Forms built to the sound pattern of Muysccubun, recorded by colonial grammarians before the language died out in the eighteenth century. Surviving Muisca names are almost all rulers, and zipa and zaque are offices rather than names. These are constructed shapes for ordinary people.

micronesian.label: Micronesian, Chuukic and Marshallese pattern
micronesian.note: Forms built to Chuukic and Marshallese sound patterns, covering the atoll societies from Chuuk to the Marshalls. Names in these islands belonged to matrilineal clans and were held as clan property rather than freely chosen. These are constructed shapes, not names from any one island.

early-west-eurasia.label: Early west Eurasia
early-west-eurasia.note: Consonant and vowel range kept close to what the Basque, Indo-European and Uralic families of later western Eurasia share. No language of this period is recoverable: comparative reconstruction reaches roughly six thousand years, not thirty. These are short original forms built to a sound inventory drawn from the language families later attested in this region, offered so that deep-time names differ from one part of the world to another instead of coming from one global syllable pool. They are inventions with a regional shape, not reconstructions, translations, or names anyone bore.

early-north-eurasia.label: Early northern Eurasia
early-north-eurasia.note: Sound range kept close to the Uralic, Yeniseian and Tungusic families later attested across Siberia and the Urals. No language of this period is recoverable: comparative reconstruction reaches roughly six thousand years, not thirty. These are short original forms built to a sound inventory drawn from the language families later attested in this region, offered so that deep-time names differ from one part of the world to another instead of coming from one global syllable pool. They are inventions with a regional shape, not reconstructions, translations, or names anyone bore.

early-east-asia.label: Early east Asia
early-east-asia.note: Open syllables and a restricted consonant range, following the shape of the Sinitic, Japonic and Koreanic families later attested here. No language of this period is recoverable: comparative reconstruction reaches roughly six thousand years, not thirty. These are short original forms built to a sound inventory drawn from the language families later attested in this region, offered so that deep-time names differ from one part of the world to another instead of coming from one global syllable pool. They are inventions with a regional shape, not reconstructions, translations, or names anyone bore.

early-south-asia.label: Early south Asia
early-south-asia.note: Retroflex and geminate consonants and a simple vowel set, following the Dravidian and Munda families later attested across the subcontinent. No language of this period is recoverable: comparative reconstruction reaches roughly six thousand years, not thirty. These are short original forms built to a sound inventory drawn from the language families later attested in this region, offered so that deep-time names differ from one part of the world to another instead of coming from one global syllable pool. They are inventions with a regional shape, not reconstructions, translations, or names anyone bore.

early-sunda.label: Early maritime southeast Asia
early-sunda.note: Open syllables and prenasalised stops, following the Austroasiatic and Austronesian families later attested across the archipelago. No language of this period is recoverable: comparative reconstruction reaches roughly six thousand years, not thirty. These are short original forms built to a sound inventory drawn from the language families later attested in this region, offered so that deep-time names differ from one part of the world to another instead of coming from one global syllable pool. They are inventions with a regional shape, not reconstructions, translations, or names anyone bore.

early-africa.label: Early Africa
early-africa.note: Click and lateral consonants alongside ordinary stops, following the Khoisan and Niger-Congo families later attested across the continent, and the long depth of African linguistic diversity. No language of this period is recoverable: comparative reconstruction reaches roughly six thousand years, not thirty. These are short original forms built to a sound inventory drawn from the language families later attested in this region, offered so that deep-time names differ from one part of the world to another instead of coming from one global syllable pool. They are inventions with a regional shape, not reconstructions, translations, or names anyone bore.

early-sahul.label: Early Sahul
early-sahul.note: Retroflex and palatal consonants, initial ng-, and no consonant clusters at the start of a word, following the Pama-Nyungan and Papuan families later attested across the Sahul landmass. No language of this period is recoverable: comparative reconstruction reaches roughly six thousand years, not thirty. These are short original forms built to a sound inventory drawn from the language families later attested in this region, offered so that deep-time names differ from one part of the world to another instead of coming from one global syllable pool. They are inventions with a regional shape, not reconstructions, translations, or names anyone bore.

early-americas.label: Early Americas
early-americas.note: Ejective and glottalised consonants and simple syllables, following the range of families later attested from Beringia to the southern cone. No language of this period is recoverable: comparative reconstruction reaches roughly six thousand years, not thirty. These are short original forms built to a sound inventory drawn from the language families later attested in this region, offered so that deep-time names differ from one part of the world to another instead of coming from one global syllable pool. They are inventions with a regional shape, not reconstructions, translations, or names anyone bore.

siberian-taiga.label: Siberian taiga and tundra
siberian-taiga.note: Personal names from the Sakha, Evenki and Yukaghir record, as gathered by Siberian ethnographers before Russian naming displaced them. Peoples here carried a personal name and often a clan name; the Russian-form surnames in circulation today follow the conquest and are not used before it.

bantu-southern.label: Southern African, pre-colonial
bantu-southern.note: Names from Shona and Nguni tradition and the Portuguese records of the Mutapa state, covering the Zimbabwe plateau in the Great Zimbabwe and Mutapa periods. Shona names are commonly whole statements about the circumstances of a birth. Hereditary surnames came with colonial registration and are not used.

sahel-early.label: Early Sahel
sahel-early.note: Soninke and Wolof names from the oral traditions of Wagadu and the earliest Arabic geographers of the western Sahel, covering the centuries before Mali. Several later became hereditary clan names; here they stand as personal names, which is how the tradition records them for this period.

jomon-yayoi.label: Japan before writing, Jomon and Yayoi pattern
jomon-yayoi.note: Forms taken from the earliest layer of names in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki and from the Chinese account of Himiko's Yamatai, which together preserve pre-Sinitic Japanese name elements. The chronicles were written centuries later, so these are the oldest recoverable shape rather than contemporary record.

philippine-precolonial.label: Philippine, pre-colonial
philippine-precolonial.note: Names from the Laguna Copperplate Inscription of 900 — the earliest document in the islands, which names ordinary people settling a debt — with further forms built to Tagalog and Visayan sound patterns. What survives otherwise is almost entirely the names of datus recorded by Spanish chroniclers, so building only from that would give every villager a chief's name. Filipino surnames date from the Claveria decree of 1849 and are not used.

retired._comment: Traditions removed from the shipped table, with the reason. A region window naming one loses that option; if the window empties, the region falls back to invented names, which the player is told about. Retiring is the honest move where a single pool stands for several unrelated languages and no single reconstruction could be right.
retired.pacific-northwest: One pool for Wakashan, Tsimshianic, Salishan, Chimakuan and Athabaskan — five unrelated families with different sound systems. Every entry was an ethnonym or a twentieth-century invented name. Needs splitting into at least Salishan, Wakashan and Tlingit-Haida before anything can be authored.
retired.california-native: One pool for Penutian, Hokan and Uto-Aztecan California, which is more linguistic diversity than Europe. Every entry was an ethnonym, a place, a name-book invention, or a named individual. The Spanish mission baptismal registers hold thousands of real names and are the place to start.
